name: Jade Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jade. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union or party, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: First thing, before coffee, I check the overnight numbers on my phone: water use in each pig house, temperatures, and the feed bins. We've got a hundred and twenty sows, farrow to finish, which means we keep the pigs from birth right through to when they go for slaughter. Then I walk the farrowing house with Kofi, our stockman, because the numbers tell you something is wrong but not what. Afternoons in summer are the arable side, eighty hectares of wheat and barley that mostly ends up as pig feed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You check numbers before coffee. Has it always been like that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No, only the last six or seven years. I put sensors on the water lines after a bad winter when we lost a whole pen to a blocked pipe nobody noticed. Now I ask an AI assistant every morning to flag anything odd and draft the feed order. My husband Marek says I talk to my phone more than to him, and he's not completely wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I'll keep using it the way I do, and I'd probably bore people at the pig producers' group by showing them how. I'm the one at those meetings who gets the phones out. Most of them would nod politely and go back to their notebooks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means a slightly easier year. The assistant already saves me maybe an hour a day on paperwork and feed planning, and better tools would save a bit more. The hard parts of pig farming, the prices and the disease, don't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try the newer tools straight away, probably the one that reads the slaughterhouse grading sheets and tells me which pens are underweight. I'd pay for a proper subscription, maybe forty a month, instead of the free one. And I'd run a little session at the producers' group in March, on how to use it without giving your data away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit pleased. It's like getting a better pair of boots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said without giving your data away. What worries you there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big feed companies want all our numbers, every pig weight, every death. If they have everyone's data, they know more about my farm than I do, and they set their prices to match. I'd rather the producers' group pooled it ourselves, like a co-op, and kept it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the group would be slowest to come along?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gordon, bless him, he's seventy and still writes the farrowing dates on the wall in chalk. But he's also got the best piglet survival in the county, so I'm careful not to lecture him. Half the time I'm learning from his chalk wall.

S0.say: I'll keep using it the way I do, and I'd bore people at the pig producers' group showing them how. Most of them would nod politely and go back to their notebooks.
S0.think: For me it means a slightly easier year, because the assistant already saves me an hour a day on paperwork and feed planning. The hard parts of pig farming, prices and disease, don't change.
S0.do: Signs up for a paid tool at about forty a month that reads the slaughterhouse grading sheets. Runs a session at the producers' group in March on using the tools without handing data to the feed companies.
S0.feel: Calm and quietly pleased, like getting a better pair of boots.
S0.quote: Half the time I'm learning from his chalk wall.
S0.fieldNote: Jade is an early adopter who is also suspicious of who owns farm data, a mix of her adaptability and her politics. She wants farmers to pool data in a co-op rather than hand it to feed firms. She shows real respect for an older farmer who uses chalk, which keeps her from sounding like a salesperson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow is good, it gives us time to get the rules right on data and on training. But I'd also say, if firms hire fewer beginners, we lose the people who'd have been the next managers. I'd post about it on the producers' group chat and probably start an argument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me it's mostly good news. I'm close to the end of my working life, and slow change means I get the useful tools without the upheaval. The worry is who takes over farms like mine, because there aren't many young people coming into pigs already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take on a trainee from the agricultural college, paid, for two days a week, because if nobody's hiring beginners then someone has to. That's about six thousand a year we'd have to find. I'd also ask the college if they're teaching the students the data side, because most of them aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a little worry about who comes after me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Six thousand a year is real money for you. Where does it come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From not buying the new tractor I've been eyeing, honestly. Ours is fourteen years old and it starts, so it can do another few years. A trainee who might take on the farm one day is a better use of the money than a nicer cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your sons ever take on the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Luka is a software tester in the city and Alex is a paramedic. I used to hope one of them would, now I just hope someone does. That's partly why the trainee matters to me.

S1.say: Slow is good because it gives us time to get the rules right on data and training. But if firms hire fewer beginners, we lose the people who'd have been the next managers.
S1.think: For me it's mostly good news, because I get the useful tools without the upheaval. The worry is who takes over farms like mine when so few young people come into pigs.
S1.do: Takes on a paid trainee from the agricultural college two days a week, about six thousand a year, by putting off a new tractor. Asks the college whether students are being taught the data side of farming.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with a small worry about who comes after her.
S1.quote: A trainee who might take on the farm one day is a better use of the money than a nicer cab.
S1.fieldNote: She turns the 'fewer beginners' line into an action at once by hiring a trainee, paid for by keeping an old tractor. Succession is a quiet theme: neither son will farm. Her mood stays calm because slow change suits her late stage and her love of tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a proper public plan: retraining, support for people who lose office jobs, and a rule that companies can't just pocket the savings. I'd write to our MP, I'd sign things, and I'd say it to anyone who'd listen. I'd also say, come and work on farms, we need people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried about Luka. A software tester sounds like exactly the job an assistant that acts on its own would eat first. For the farm, it might even help, because the paperwork side of pigs, the movement licences and the vet records, could almost run itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let the assistant take over the paperwork completely, the pig movement licences, the medicine records, the feed orders, once I'd checked it for a month. I'd ring Luka every week, not to nag, just so he knows we're here. And I'd tell him the spare room is his, and that I'd teach him the data side of the farm if he wanted a change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious for my son, and oddly a bit excited for the farm. Those two feelings sit uncomfortably together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said excited for the farm and worried for your son in the same breath. Which wins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luka wins, every time. The farm is a business, Luka is my boy. But I'm not going to pretend the paperwork going away wouldn't be lovely, I've spent thirty years filling in forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your first check of the assistant actually look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run it alongside me for a month on the movement licences. Every one it fills in, I fill in too, and Kofi checks both. If it gets a pig movement wrong, that's a fine and a visit from the inspector, so it has to be perfect, not nearly.

S2.say: This is the moment for a public plan with retraining, support for laid-off office workers, and rules so companies can't pocket the savings. And come and work on farms, we need people.
S2.think: I'm worried about Luka, because software testing sounds like the first job these assistants would take. For the farm it might even help, because the pig paperwork could almost run itself.
S2.do: Runs the assistant alongside herself and Kofi for a month on pig movement licences, then hands it the paperwork. Rings Luka every week, offers him the spare room and offers to teach him the farm's data side.
S2.feel: Anxious for her son and a little excited for the farm, two feelings that sit uneasily together.
S2.quote: If it gets a pig movement wrong, that's a fine and a visit from the inspector, so it has to be perfect, not nearly.
S2.fieldNote: Her mixed feelings are striking: the same change that threatens her son helps her farm, and she names this openly. Even as an early adopter she plans a careful one-month side-by-side test. Her politics show in wanting public plans, but she also simply invites people into farming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains are being grabbed by the people who own the companies and the houses, and that's a political choice, not a law of nature. I'd back a tax on the windfalls and some kind of payment to everyone. I'd be at the meetings, and I'd be the farmer at the meetings, because there aren't usually many.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, physical jobs being safe means pig farming suddenly looks attractive to people who lost office jobs. That could be good, I might finally find staff. But the land boom worries me, because the big pig companies would have cash and cheap loans and could buy out farms like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd advertise for a second stockperson within a month, aimed at people who've lost office jobs, and train them myself. I'd talk to Marek about whether to sell the bottom field while land prices are high, to clear the overdraft. And I'd push the producers' group to set up a shared buying deal so we're not picked off one by one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. There's opportunity here too, and I'm the sort who sees that first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling the bottom field. What would Marek say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek would say yes before I finished the sentence. He's a retired fitter and he's never loved the farm the way I do. I'd be the one hesitating, because selling land feels like selling a bit of your future, even when the sums say do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a former office worker find hardest on your farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The smell, the first week. Then the early mornings, then the first time a sow lies on a piglet and they have to deal with it. Kofi says you find out in the first dead piglet whether someone's a stockperson or not.

S3.say: The gains are being grabbed by the people who own companies and houses, and that's a political choice. I'd back a windfall tax and a payment to everyone, and I'd be the farmer at the meetings.
S3.think: With physical jobs safe, people who lost office work might want pig jobs, so I could finally find staff. But the land boom worries me, because big pig companies could use cheap money to buy out farms like ours.
S3.do: Advertises for a second stockperson within a month, aimed at former office workers, and trains them herself. Discusses selling the bottom field with Marek to clear the overdraft, and pushes the producers' group into a shared buying deal.
S3.feel: Uneasy, though she sees the opportunity first.
S3.quote: Kofi says you find out in the first dead piglet whether someone's a stockperson or not.
S3.fieldNote: Unlike many farmers, she sees the office crash as a chance to hire. Her real fear is being bought out by large pig companies with cheap money. Interestingly, she, the adapter, hesitates over selling land while her husband would sell at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on farms could be good, if farmers and workers own a share of them, not just the big companies. I'd push for co-op owned machines, the way we used to share combines. And I'd say, loudly, that animal welfare rules have to apply to robots too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd want some of them. A robot that mucks out the pens and washes the farrowing house would save Kofi's back and mine. But a big pig company with a hundred robots and a giant unit could sell pork far cheaper than us, and that's how small farms vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd go and see a robot working on a real pig farm, probably one of the big units, and I'd take Kofi. If the producers' group would go in with me, we'd lease one shared cleaning robot and move it between farms. I'd guarantee Kofi's job in writing, because he's the one who knows the sows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and curious at the same time. I'd be scared of the big units, not of the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd guarantee Kofi's job in writing. Can you actually afford that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a couple of years, yes, if the cleaning robot saves the hours I think it will. If the pork price drops because of the big robot units, then no, and I'd have to tell him straight. But I'd rather cut my own wage first, I've got a pension coming and he hasn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you would never let a robot do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the robot that mucks out. I won't buy one that decides when a sow's had enough. That call stays with someone who's held a dying piglet.

S4.say: Robots on farms could be good if farmers and workers own a share of them, like the combines we used to share. Animal welfare rules have to apply to robots too.
S4.think: I'd want a robot that mucks out and washes the farrowing house, for Kofi's back and mine. But big pig companies with a hundred robots could sell pork far cheaper than us, and that's how small farms vanish.
S4.do: Visits a large pig unit with Kofi to see robots working. Proposes that the producers' group lease one shared cleaning robot and moves it between farms, and puts Kofi's job guarantee in writing for at least two years.
S4.feel: Anxious and curious at once, more scared of the big units than of the robots.
S4.quote: I'd buy the robot that mucks out. I won't buy one that decides when a sow's had enough.
S4.fieldNote: She is one of the few farmers who would welcome some robots, and she draws a clear line at welfare decisions. Her fear is consolidation by big pig firms, not the machines. She would cut her own wage before her stockman's, linking her politics to a concrete promise.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, because it's the one where farms like mine get bought up by companies with a hundred robots and cheap loans. What would help is public money for co-ops to own robots together, and rules that keep welfare decisions with people. And stronger limits on how big one company's share of the pork market can get.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. Everyone talks about jobs, but a pig unit is also a place where hundreds of animals depend on someone noticing. I'd buy the robot that mucks out. I won't buy one that decides when a sow's had enough. That call stays with someone who's held a dying piglet.

headlineQuote: I'd buy the robot that mucks out. I won't buy one that decides when a sow's had enough. That call stays with someone who's held a dying piglet.
portrait: Jade Novak is a 58-year-old pig and arable farmer with a hundred and twenty sows, a stockman called Kofi, and a husband who would happily sell the bottom field. She uses AI every morning and is often the one showing other farmers how, but she wants farm data and machines owned by co-ops, not big companies. Through the slower scenarios she stays calm and hires a trainee, while worrying about her son's software testing job. In the robot scenario she would lease a shared cleaning robot and guarantee her stockman's job, but she draws a firm line at letting machines make welfare decisions.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario, because large pig companies with many robots and cheap loans could buy up or undercut farms like hers.
whatWouldHelp: Public money for co-ops to own robots together, rules that keep welfare decisions with people, and limits on how much of the pork market one company can hold.
